shows.title: Color Songs: Musicians as Visual Artists
shows.description:
Color Songs takes as its premise a simple but rich idea: that the same creative impulse can move between sound and image, and that musicians who paint or draw are working out on canvas something related to what they work out on an instrument. Curated by Dr. Yaoundé Olu — herself a visual artist, musician, and longtime fixture of Chicago's Black arts scene — the show gathers painters, sculptors, printmakers, and fiber artists who also make music, alongside musicians for whom visual art is a second, parallel practice.

The exhibition centers on two figures with especially vivid double lives. Sura Dupart, a sculptor and one of the original Sun Drummers, contributes foam-and-acrylic sculptures built with the same rhythmic sensibility he brings to performance at Hyde Park's Woodlawn Tap. The late Carol Sawall, a painter in oils, acrylics, and watercolor who also recorded her own music, is represented by canvases that have circulated in private collections for years. Around them, a wider group of artist-musicians fills out the fourth-floor gallery with paintings, drawings, mixed media, and photography.

It's a loose, generous curatorial frame — pieces don't have to depict music, just come from someone who lives in both disciplines — and that looseness gives the show a scrapbook energy, jumping between styles and media in a way that mirrors how creative people actually work across their lives. Worth a look for anyone curious how a life in sound bleeds into a life in paint.

shows.title: GuruShots Photo Exhibition: Chicago 2026
shows.description:
GuruShots is a crowdsourced photography platform that runs daily themed challenges for photographers worldwide, and this exhibition is the print-and-frame payoff: 150 images pulled from those online contests, submitted by photographers from more than thirty countries and printed for the third-floor gallery wall.

Because the source material comes from open online challenges rather than a single curatorial vision, the range is wide — landscapes, night photography, portraiture, street scenes, abstraction — unified mainly by the fact that each image won its category against a global pool of entrants. The result reads less like a traditional thematic show and more like a highlight reel of contemporary amateur and semi-pro photography from around the world, heavy on dramatic light and striking single-frame compositions.

It's an easy, browsable show — good for anyone who wants a broad survey of what's winning attention in online photo communities right now, condensed into one room.

shows.title: Return to Nature
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this under "Current Exhibitions" with no run dates given, only its location: "5th Floor Gallery Shared Floor Ceramics."
shows.description:
Park Yon-jae, a Korean visual designer who has taught industrial design at Joongbu University for over two decades, brings an illustrator's eye to this print-on-canvas series about escaping an over-mediated, barcode-saturated world. Fish, butterflies, and flowers stand in for a human self trying to swim back toward something unspoiled — the show's title, Return to Nature, is meant fairly literally.

It's Park's eleventh solo exhibition, and the work leans on the clean, graphic language of commercial design (Park's day job) bent toward a more personal, almost devotional theme. The barcode-versus-butterfly contrast is blunt, but it gives the images an immediate, poster-like clarity — appropriate for a show installed in the light-filled Shared Floor Ceramics space on Bridgeport's fifth floor.

Worth a stop for anyone interested in how a career in design translates into a fine-art practice, or in the shared-studio ceramics scene where the show is installed.

shows.title: Art Connection: Past Meets Present
shows.description:
This is a show built around a relationship rather than a medium or a theme: the bond between art teachers and the students they've shaped. Presented by ArtConnectED, Art Connection: Past Meets Present pairs work by educators with work by their former students, tracing how a lesson learned in a classroom keeps unfolding years later in an independent studio practice.

The premise gives the exhibition an unusually personal structure — rather than a single curatorial thesis about style or subject, each pairing tells its own small story of mentorship. Awards, underwritten by Blick Art Materials and a roster of partnering art schools and colleges, add a competitive layer for the participating alumni. Expect a wide spread of media and skill levels, from students still early in their practice to educators with decades of exhibition history.

It's a generous, community-minded show, less about connoisseurship than about making visible the usually invisible chain of influence that runs through art education — worth a visit for anyone who's ever had a teacher who mattered.

shows.title: Una Vuelta a Mis Raíces (A Return to My Roots): Monochromatic Pigment Paintings
shows.description:
Robert Lipton's mixed-media paintings work the way sediment works — through accumulation. Layer upon layer of pigment and organic material builds up into thick, cracked, geological-looking surfaces that owe an open debt to Antoni Tàpies, Anselm Kiefer, and Bosco Sodi, artists for whom the physical body of a painting carries as much meaning as its image.

The monochromatic palette forces attention onto texture and process rather than color relationships: fissures, ridges, and pooled material read almost like aerial views of eroded terrain or cracked earth. Titled around the idea of returning to one's roots, the series treats the act of building up a painted surface as a kind of excavation in reverse — constructing a landscape rather than uncovering one.

It's a quiet, materials-first show that rewards close, slow looking rather than a quick pass, installed in Bridgeport's third-floor gallery.

shows.title: Between Memory and Becoming: Manifestations of Black Motherhood
shows.artist: Alexy Irving-Alleyne, Andrea Hill Fitzgerald, Grandeast Wright, Summer Coleman, and Teni Odunsi
shows.description:
This is the culminating show for a two-year artist cohort experience: five Black mother-artists who came up through WILD YAMS' SEED Residency, a Chicago South Side program built specifically to support Black mothers and caretakers in sustaining a creative practice alongside the demands of parenting. The exhibition gathers what they made across that residency — sculpture, photography, painting, text, and mixed media — around the shared, unresolved subject of Black motherhood.

Rather than a single argument about what mothering means, the show works more like a chorus: each artist traces her own line between the natural world, diasporic tradition, and the day-to-day practices of survival and care that rarely get named as art-making. An interactive installation, "Word to Your Mother," invites visitors into that conversation directly, and the show's framing pointedly resists tidy narratives — motherhood here is presented as unfixed, plural, and still being formed rather than a fixed role to honor or resolve.

It's a rare kind of show in that its premise is inseparable from its process: the work exists because a residency was built to make space for it, and that context (funded jointly by Co-Prosperity and the Crossroads Fund) shapes how the pieces read together. Programming around the exhibition includes an artists' talk and a Lumpen Radio series extending the conversation about Black motherhood beyond the gallery walls.

shows.title: A Creature Who Is Aware of Joy and Despair and Everything in Between
shows.description:
For her first solo show, Katharine Joy Houpt has done something structurally unusual: instead of hanging work inside the gallery, she's built a thirty-foot anthropomorphic creature out of ten quilted panels and installed it across the windows of the Co-Prosperity Sphere, turning the building's own facade into the body of the piece. Passersby on Morgan Street become the show's unintended first audience, seeing the creature's fragmented form from the sidewalk before anyone steps inside.

Houpt works slowly and improvisationally, piecing together found and reused fabric through free-motion quilting, appliqué, trapunto, and embroidery — techniques that let the material itself suggest who the creature becomes rather than working from a fixed plan. The result draws visibly on the tradition of the Chicago Imagists, with their appetite for grotesque, comic, and tender bodies existing in the same image, but translated into a slow textile process more associated with domestic craft than gallery sculpture.

The title is the clearest guide to what's going on inside the piece: this is a work about holding contradictory emotional registers — awe and disappointment, humor and rage — at once, without resolving them into a single mood. Houpt has an MA in Art Therapy from SAIC and taught there for a decade; that background shows in how attentively the piece treats the creature's "inner world" as something worth taking seriously rather than as pure whimsy. It's an ambitious, site-specific debut and one of the more visually startling things on view in Chicago's gallery scene this month.

shows.title: Dazzle Pig
shows.description:
Connie Wilson's Dazzle Pig turns a barnyard animal into a study in surface and disguise. Made from deadstock fabric stretched over MDF, her pig sculptures come in a run of variations — Dumb Pig, Deliberate Pig, Ditsy Pig, Dead Pig — each named for a different register of personality, as if the same basic form kept getting recast through mood rather than anatomy. A parallel series of small balsa-wood and foam-core "Pig House" structures, finished with gesso, acrylic, and ribbon, reads like dollhouse architecture built for the same animal.

The title borrows from "dazzle camouflage," the disruptive geometric paint schemes used on WWI ships to confuse enemy sight lines rather than hide the ship outright — a fitting reference for work more interested in surface pattern and misdirection than in naturalistic representation. Wilson, who is originally from Belfast and trained at NSCAD and the University of Guelph, has been showing internationally in Vienna, Zürich, Montreal, and Toronto; this Chicago outing continues her interest in taking a familiar, almost cartoonish subject and running it through variations until the repetition itself becomes the point.

It's a tightly focused, single-subject show — good for anyone who likes to watch an artist wring every possible mood out of one simple form.

shows.title: My Little Pictures
shows.dates_note: Venue's own site confirms the show is currently on view (homepage banner links to a "Show and Tell" event with the artist on September 12, 2026) but publishes no opening or closing date for the exhibition itself.
shows.description:
James Hall's first solo show in twelve years is really three bodies of work orbiting the same restless imagination. A Maze of Wormholes is the most immediately striking: twelve pencil-drawn panels of forking, knotting tubes that read like blueprints for an impossible machine. Alongside it sits 35 Years of What I Wanted to Remember, a handmade artist book built from decades of collected packaging, advertisements, and printed ephemera — xeroxed, then hand-colored with vibrant pencil gradients until the found material becomes something entirely Hall's own.

The show's third strand is the most personal: more than five hundred small 2"x4" ink drawings made between 2012 and 2021, born out of Hall's counseling sessions around his schizophrenia. He has described the pictures as a way of releasing emotion and building a private method of recovery, and the range on view — surreal one moment, quotidian the next — adds up to an unusually candid self-portrait built one tiny image at a time.

Hall (b. 1954) works across ink, graphite, acrylic, collage, and assemblage, and this show's real achievement is holding all of it together — the cosmic wormhole drawings, the pop-art scrapbook, the diaristic ink miniatures — as facets of one restless, inquisitive mind. A companion publication of the "35 Years" book accompanies the exhibition.

shows.title: Forever Yours: A Celebration of Tattooing
shows.artist: Ken Bortman, Ruby Bradford, Bill Douglas, Adam Hines, Fernando Ramirez, Lainey Sears, Noon Slaps, Luke Shemroske, and Alita Van Hee
shows.description:
Nine Project Onward artists turn their attention to tattoo culture — its imagery, its flash-sheet conventions, and its permanence — translating a body art form into drawings, paintings, and mixed-media work made to hang on a wall instead of skin. Rather than illustrating tattoos from the outside, several artists have designed original flash sheets in their own distinctive styles, treating the tattoo shop's stock-image tradition as raw material for personal invention.

The group brings very different sensibilities to a shared subject: expect everything from Ken Bortman's meticulous fragments to Noon Slaps' intuitive, cellular abstraction and Fernando Ramirez's documentary eye, all filtered through the visual shorthand of traditional tattoo art — hearts, banners, roses, skulls — recombined into each artist's own vocabulary.

It's a lively, image-dense group show and a good entry point into Project Onward's roster for anyone unfamiliar with the studio, which supports Chicago-based artists living with mental illness and developmental disabilities.

shows.title: All Terrain: The Contemporary Landscape
shows.artist: Joan Holleb, Michael Dubina, Mark Flickinger, Paula Blackwell, Julia Katz, Karen Perl, Misha Goro, Brooks Anderson, Robin Denevan, Marie Renaudin, and Dag Hol
shows.dates_note: Gallery site lists an opening reception of Friday, July 10, 2026 for this current group show but publishes no closing date.
shows.description:
Eleven painters share the walls of Addington Gallery for this survey of how contemporary artists keep reinventing landscape as a subject. The through-line is process as much as place: Joan Holleb pours patina solutions onto sheets of copper and paints into the chemical reaction, letting oxidation dictate the compositions that emerge, while Robin Denevan builds his river and horizon scenes out of layered beeswax, resin, and oil on etched wood panel. Michael Dubina and Mark Flickinger work in a more direct plein-air-influenced mode, with Flickinger's small, tightly observed oil studies of forest paths and waterfalls sitting alongside Dubina's warmer, more symbolic fields and skies.

Karen Perl's contribution continues her long-running series of Chicago street corners rendered through a veil of gray, images built from repeated repainting until a half-remembered version of the place settles into view. Paula Blackwell's encaustic landscapes and the rest of the roster - Julia Katz, Misha Goro, Brooks Anderson, Marie Renaudin, and Dag Hol - round out a show that treats "landscape" loosely enough to include invented, atmospheric, and emotionally coded terrain alongside more legible depictions of woods, rivers, and city corners.

It's a low-key, dealer-gallery survey rather than a thematically tight curatorial statement, but that's part of the appeal: eleven working painters, many with decades in the medium, given a few pieces each to make their case for why landscape remains worth returning to.

shows.title: Sundowning
shows.description:
Kevin Blake's solo show, curated by Dan Cameron, gathers a decade of the Chicago painter's densely worked figure drawings — graphite, oil pastel, oil paint, and collage built up on paper mounted to canvas, most around 30 x 22 inches. The titles are as loaded as the imagery: works like "A Third Degree Witness," "Broad by Breed," and "With a Pound of Platinum on His Famished Hands" read like fragments of a private vocabulary, hinting at the psychological weight behind each composition.

Blake grew up on Chicago's far South Side in a family with generations in the police department, and his work since studying painting at SAIC has circled back repeatedly to the inherited codes of masculinity, authority, and violence he absorbed there. The figures in these pieces are worked over so many times — in graphite, oil, pastel, sometimes colored pencil — that faces and bodies start to blur into something closer to wound or residue than portrait, a fitting register for an artist examining what gets passed down and what might be undone.

The show's title suggests both a literal decline (the confusion associated with sundowning) and a broader reckoning with inherited identity as daylight fades on it. It's a tightly focused solo presentation, useful as an introduction to an artist who has been building this body of work steadily since the late 2010s, and it opens alongside Chicago Exhibition Week, with a closing artist talk scheduled for mid-October.

shows.title: Latinitudes: A Collection of Latin American Modern Architecture
shows.artist: Leonardo Finotti (curated by Michelle Jean de Castro)
shows.description:
Brazilian photographer Leonardo Finotti spent years traveling to twelve Latin American cities - from Havana to Buenos Aires, Mexico City to Santiago - documenting the housing blocks, civic buildings, and cultural centers built by the region's modernist architects: Luis Barragán, Lina Bo Bardi, Oscar Niemeyer, Roberto Burle Marx, Félix Candela, and others. More than 100 of those photographs, printed as monochrome images on aluminum composite panels, fill two floors of the Graham Foundation's Madlener House for this show, making its U.S. debut after touring venues across Latin America and Europe.

Curator Michelle Jean de Castro organizes the photographs geographically rather than chronologically or by architect, running the exhibition "south to north by latitude" and hanging every image along a single continuous horizon line at eye level. The device nods to Joaquín Torres-García's inverted map of the Americas and his insistence that "our north is the south" - an explicit rejection of the usual hierarchy that puts North American and European modernism at the center of the story.

Seen together, the photographs make the case that Latin American modernism developed as its own confident, interconnected tradition rather than a derivative echo of Europe or the United States. For a city as invested in its own architectural mythology as Chicago, the show (organized in partnership with the Chicago Architecture Biennial) is a useful corrective, and a rare chance to see this scale of documentation of the region's built environment in one room.

shows.title: Tangible Sound: Arrival to a Higher Ground
shows.artist: Lauren Deutsch and Jonathan Woods (with the Tangible Sound Collaborative)
shows.description:
Photographer Lauren Deutsch has spent 45 years documenting Chicago's creative improvised music scene, and this exhibition turns that archive into an immersive tribute to the city's jazz avant-garde. Working with filmmaker Jonathan Woods and the Tangible Sound Collaborative, Deutsch translates decades of performance photography, much of it tied to the AACM and its circle, into a multi-sensory installation that pairs images with movement and color rather than presenting them as a straightforward photo survey.

The show is dedicated to two figures central to that history: community organizer and educator Timuel D. Black and bassist and mentor Fred Anderson, both of whom shaped Chicago's improvised-music community well beyond the bandstand. Programming around the exhibition includes ancestor-honoring events and musician talks that extend the show's premise that jazz photography is also a form of oral history.

For anyone who thinks of Chicago's jazz legacy as a strictly musical story, this is a reminder that the scene has always had its own visual culture - photographers, filmmakers, and now installation artists working alongside the musicians to document and extend the tradition.

shows.title: The Big Picture: Midwest Large Format Asylum — Large Format Photography
shows.description:
Organized by the Midwest Large Format Asylum, an association of photographers committed to keeping view-camera traditions alive, this group show fills the Cultural Center's Renaissance Court with more than 70 prints spanning historic and contemporary large-format practice. The work ranges from straight landscape and portraiture to still life and abstraction, but the connecting thread is process: every image here starts with a large-format camera and the slow, deliberate workflow that requires, from ground-glass focusing to sheet film.

At a moment when digital capture and AI-generated imagery dominate how pictures get made, the show is an argument for slowness and material presence — for photographs that carry the evidence of hand, light, and chemistry rather than algorithmic processing. A companion program of talks and demonstrations runs alongside the exhibition, including a wet-plate collodion demonstration and a hands-on cyanotype workshop, giving visitors a chance to see the processes behind the prints in action.

It's a craft-forward, community-organized show rather than a tightly curated single statement, and it rewards visitors willing to look closely at how differently more than 40 photographers from Chicago and the greater Midwest handle the same basic technical constraints.

shows.title: Urban Grain
shows.description:
Sculptural street artist CLs (Charles L. Shriver) brings a solo show of urban-inspired sculptural work to this South Loop storefront gallery, timed to Chicago Exhibition Week. The title points to Shriver's core material interest: the textures, patterns, and built-up surfaces of city environments, translated into dimensional pieces rather than flat street-art imagery.

Elephant Room has built its program around exactly this kind of local, emerging talent for over a decade, and a solo sculptural presentation is a change of pace from the painting-heavy group shows the gallery often runs. Expect work that reads as an extension of Shriver's public-facing street practice, reworked at gallery scale and finish.

The show opens with an evening reception and continues with a full Saturday open house the following day before settling into the gallery's regular Friday-Saturday hours through the end of October.

shows.title: Cydney Lewis: Reflection
shows.description:
Cydney Lewis builds her collages and sculptural assemblages out of material most people would throw away: packaging, plastic bags, magazine cutouts, discarded ephemera she encounters around her South Side Chicago neighborhood. For Reflection, that scavenging practice gets folded into Streetside, Lewis's ongoing project of layering hand-cut collage with digital drawing made on her phone during commutes and downtime, work that circles around Black consumer culture and the rhythms of everyday urban life.

Lewis trained as an architect - a BS from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, study at L'École d'Architecture de Versailles - before her practice pulled toward multimedia collage and assemblage, and that spatial background shows up in how she constructs these works, treating found material like building components rather than just source imagery. She's also spent time in ballet and film, disciplines that inform the sense of motion and layering running through the work.

Presented in the gallery's main space through mid-December, Reflection gives Chicago audiences an extended look at an artist who has been steadily building a reputation through shows at Hyde Park Art Center and the Ukrainian Institute of Modern Art, among others, and who treats the discarded material of the city as a starting point for renewal rather than waste.

shows.title: Press & Pull: A Legacy of the Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop
shows.artist: Group exhibition (Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop artists)
shows.description:
This traveling survey (originating at the James Gallery, CUNY Graduate Center, and passing through MassArt Art Museum before arriving at UIC) traces the history of the Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop, founded in 1947 as one of the first racially integrated, cooperative print shops in the country. Robert Blackburn started the Workshop after the WPA's Federal Art Project dissolved, filling a gap left for artists of color who had few other places to access professional printmaking equipment and mentorship.

The show's core is 38 prints made at the Workshop itself, alongside archival ephemera and video, spanning generations of artists who passed through the space: Romare Bearden, Elizabeth Catlett, Charles White, Faith Ringgold, Martin Puryear, Chakaia Booker, Baseera Khan, and dozens more. An additional 45 prints drawn from Chicago's own printmaking history - the South Side Community Art Center, the Black Arts Movement, the Chicago Printers Guild - sit alongside the Blackburn material to draw out parallels between New York's and Chicago's print cultures.

The exhibition also incorporates footage from The Only Thing That Lasts, an oral history documentary built from interviews with artists and cultural workers connected to the Workshop across its many decades. Curated by Shameekia Shantel Johnson with a team of UIC-affiliated collaborators, it's a rare chance to see this much of the Blackburn Workshop's output in one place, framed specifically through a Chicago lens.

shows.title: Honoring Resilience: Tragedy, Memory and Honor
shows.dates_note: Gallery's own site confirms the opening reception Friday, September 11, 2026, timed to the 25th anniversary of 9/11, but publishes no closing date; a third-party listing (Chicago Gallery News) cites Oct 25, 2026 but this is unconfirmed on the venue's own page.
shows.description:
Gallery VICTOR marks the 25th anniversary of September 11 with a single-work exhibition built around Bruno Surdo's Tragedy, Memory and Honor, a five-panel painting measuring 9 by 35 feet. Surdo, a Chicago artist known for large-scale narrative figurative work, made the painting in direct response to the attacks and their aftermath, and the piece has previously been shown at the Daley Center in 2002 and 2003, earning Surdo a letter of appreciation from then-Mayor Richard M. Daley.

The exhibition expands well beyond the painting itself: artifacts Surdo collected from Ground Zero while assisting cleanup efforts two weeks after 9/11, preparatory drawings and sketches, a video documenting the painting's creation, photography, and testimonials are all included, turning the gallery into something closer to a memorial installation than a conventional painting show.

Showing the work in Surdo's hometown adds a layer of meaning to a piece that has already toured galleries nationally. The show opens during the River North Design District's Fall Gallery Walk, giving the neighborhood's opening-night crowds a considerably more solemn stop on their route than most of what else is on view that evening.
